sections.title: Start here
sections.body:
Dynamics is statics with motion added. Forces that do not cancel make things speed up, slow down or turn.

There are three ways in: follow position, speed and acceleration through time; balance force against mass times acceleration; or track energy from start to finish. Energy is usually the fastest when the question does not ask about time.
pitfalls: Using an energy method when the question asks for time, or a time method when it asks only for final speed.
Forgetting that friction acts against the direction of motion.

sections.title: Kinematics
sections.body:
Kinematics describes motion without asking what causes it. Position, velocity and acceleration are linked: velocity is how fast position changes, and acceleration is how fast velocity changes.

With constant acceleration, three equations cover everything. For a projectile, treat horizontal and vertical motion separately: horizontal speed is constant, and vertical motion has gravity pulling down. On a curved path there is acceleration toward the centre even at steady speed. Spinning bodies follow the same equations with angle, angular velocity and angular acceleration.
pitfalls: Mixing units, such as km/h with m/s^{2}.
Forgetting that deceleration is a negative acceleration.

example.problem: A car brakes from 30 m/s at 6 m/s^{2}. How far does it travel before stopping?

ideas.title: Constant acceleration
ideas.text: With constant acceleration, velocity rises linearly, so the average velocity is the mean of the start and end values. Distance = average velocity × time, which is the area under the velocity-time line.

ideas.title: Projectile motion
ideas.text: Projectile motion is constant horizontal velocity combined with constant downward acceleration. On level ground the time of flight is 2 v sin(angle) / g, and the range is R = v^{2} sin(2 × angle) / g.

ideas.title: Normal and tangential components
ideas.text: Constant speed on a curve still means acceleration, because the direction of the velocity changes. The normal (centripetal) acceleration is v^{2} / r, directed toward the centre of curvature.

examples.problem: A car starts from rest and accelerates uniformly to 36 m/s in 10 s. How far does it travel in that time?
examples.steps:
Acceleration a = 36 / 10 = 3.60 m/s^{2}.

s = \frac{1}{2} a t^{2} = \frac{1}{2}(3.60)(10)^{2} = 180.0 m.

Check: average speed 18 m/s × 10 s = 180.0 m.

examples.problem: A ball is launched from level ground at 40 m/s, at 45° above the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, how far away does it land? Use g = 9.81 m/s^{2}.
examples.steps:
Time of flight = \frac{2(40) sin 45°}{9.81} = 5.77 s.

Horizontal speed = 40 cos 45° = 28.28 m/s.

Range = 28.28 × 5.77 = 163.1 m.

examples.problem: A car travels at a constant 18 m/s around a curve of radius 90 m. What is its acceleration toward the centre of the curve?

sections.title: Mass moments of inertia
sections.body:
The mass moment of inertia is a body's resistance to being spun up or slowed down. It plays the role for rotation that mass plays for straight-line motion. It depends on how much mass there is and how far that mass sits from the axis.

The handbook lists values for common shapes about their centres. To use a different parallel axis, add the mass times the square of the distance between the axes.
pitfalls: Confusing the mass moment of inertia (kg·m^{2}) with the area moment of inertia (mm^{4}).

example.problem: A 4 kg rod is 1.5 m long. Find its moment of inertia about one end.

ideas.title: Mass moment of inertia
ideas.text: For a slender rod, I = m L^{2} / 12 about its centre. The parallel axis theorem moves it to the end: I = m L^{2} / 12 + m (L/2)^{2} = m L^{2} / 3. Moving the axis away from the centre of mass always increases I.

ideas.title: Mass moment of inertia
ideas.text: For a solid disk or cylinder about its axis, I = m r^{2} / 2. A thin ring with the same mass and radius has I = m r^{2}, twice as much, because all its mass sits at the full radius.

examples.problem: A thin uniform rod has a mass of 15 kg and a length of 3 m. What is its mass moment of inertia about an axis through one end, perpendicular to the rod?
A solid uniform disk has a mass of 30 kg and a radius of 0.25 m. What is its mass moment of inertia about its central axis?

sections.title: Force and acceleration
sections.body:
Newton's second law says an unbalanced force makes a mass accelerate in the direction of that force. Draw a free body diagram exactly as in statics, but set the sum of forces equal to mass times acceleration instead of zero.

Choose axes along and perpendicular to the motion. Friction acts against motion and equals the kinetic coefficient times the normal force. For rotation about a fixed axis, the sum of moments equals the moment of inertia times the angular acceleration.
pitfalls: Using weight (N) where mass (kg) is needed, or the reverse.
Leaving out the component of weight along an incline.

example.problem: A 10 kg block is pushed along a smooth floor by a 40 N force. Find its acceleration.

ideas.title: Newton's second law
ideas.text: Newton's second law uses the net force. Kinetic friction equals the coefficient times the normal force, and on a level floor with a horizontal pull the normal force equals the weight.

ideas.title: Newton's second law
ideas.text: Resolve the weight along and perpendicular to the slope. Only the component along the slope, m g sin(angle), accelerates the block; the perpendicular component is balanced by the normal force. The mass cancels.

ideas.title: Kinetics of a rigid body
ideas.text: Rotation about a fixed axis follows the rotational form of Newton's second law: net torque = I × angular acceleration. It is the direct counterpart of F = m a.

examples.problem: A 120 kg crate is pulled along a level floor by a 700 N horizontal force. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.35. What is the acceleration of the crate? Use g = 9.81 m/s^{2}.
A block slides down a frictionless incline at 35° to the horizontal. What is its acceleration? Use g = 9.81 m/s^{2}.

examples.problem: A net torque of 60 N·m acts on a flywheel with a mass moment of inertia of 8 kg·m^{2}. What is its angular acceleration?

sections.title: Work, energy and power
sections.body:
Work is force times the distance moved in the direction of the force. Energy is the ability to do work. Kinetic energy belongs to motion, and potential energy is stored in height or in a stretched spring.

If only gravity and springs act, total mechanical energy stays the same, so you can jump straight from the start to the finish without tracking time. Friction removes energy equal to the friction force times the distance. Power is the rate of doing work. Impulse and momentum handle impacts: force times time equals the change in mass times velocity.

formulas.name: Work-energy
formulas.expr: work done = change in kinetic energy

pitfalls: Forgetting that speed is squared in kinetic energy: doubling speed quadruples the energy.
Using energy methods when the question asks for time.

example.problem: A 1,000 kg car moving at 20 m/s brakes to a stop. How much energy do the brakes absorb?

ideas.title: Conservation of energy
ideas.text: With no air resistance, mechanical energy is conserved: m g h of potential energy becomes (1/2) m v^{2} of kinetic energy. The mass cancels, so v = square root of 2 g h for any object.

ideas.title: Power and efficiency
ideas.text: Power is force times velocity in the direction of the force. At constant speed the hoist force equals the weight, so P = m g v.

ideas.title: Elastic potential energy
ideas.text: Energy is conserved: the elastic energy stored in the spring, (1/2) k x^{2}, becomes the kinetic energy of the block, (1/2) m v^{2}.

examples.problem: A 4 kg ball is dropped from rest from a height of 30 m. Ignoring air resistance, how fast is it moving just before it lands? Use g = 9.81 m/s^{2}.
examples.steps: m g h = \frac{1}{2} m v^{2}, so v = \sqrt{2 g h} = \sqrt{2(9.81)(30)} = 24.3 m/s. The 4 kg mass is not needed.

examples.problem: A hoist lifts a 2,000 kg load at a constant 1.2 m/s. What power is delivered to the load? Use g = 9.81 m/s^{2}.
A spring with a stiffness of 3,000 N/m is compressed 0.12 m and released against a 1.5 kg block on a frictionless surface. What speed does the block reach?
